context: Given the ascending array [1, 3, 6, 6, 6, 6, 6, 10, 12, 15], with indices 0 through 9, find the insertion point for target = 6. The existing 6s occupy consecutive indices 2 through 6. Return the index where a new 6 would go to the left of all existing 6s. The algorithm only computes and returns the insertion index. It does not move or insert any elements.

Pointers i and j mark the left and right boundaries of the closed search interval [i, j]. Compute the midpoint index m by rounding (i + j) / 2 down. When nums[m] < target, set i = m + 1 to move right. When nums[m] > target or nums[m] == target, set j = m − 1 to narrow the interval to the left. This brings j closer to the rightmost element less than target and i closer to the first position with a value greater than or equal to target.
description: Each iteration first computes the midpoint, then moves one boundary. Just after the boundary moves, the diagram still shows the previous midpoint m, which may lie outside the new interval. The pointer m updates only when the midpoint is recomputed.

The fixed input appears first, followed by a table tracing the pointers across eight frames. The step descriptions explain each operation and the resulting state. The eight frames cover three midpoint comparisons.

frames.announcement: Set the left boundary i = 0 and the right boundary j = 9. The closed search interval [0, 9] covers all 10 elements.
frames.explanation: The target is 6. Set i = 0 and j = 9. The closed interval [0, 9] covers all ten elements, and m has yet to be computed. See “Fixed input: Target value 6” for the array.
frames.key_state: Initialization: target 6, i = 0, j = 9, interval [0, 9]. The midpoint m has yet to be computed.
frames.title: Initialize the search interval

frames.announcement: In the closed interval [0, 9], the first midpoint is m = (0 + 9) // 2 = 4. The midpoint element nums[4] = 6 equals the target, 6.
frames.explanation: Iteration 1: With i = 0 and j = 9 in [0, 9], compute m = (0 + 9) // 2 = 4. The value nums[4] = 6 equals the target, but an earlier 6 may exist.
frames.key_state: Iteration 1 midpoint: i = 0, j = 9, interval [0, 9], m = 4, nums[4] = 6.
frames.title: Compute midpoint 4

frames.announcement: Since nums[4] = 6 equals the target, 6, keep looking for an earlier 6 to find the leftmost insertion point. Set j = m − 1 to move the right boundary left to 3. The old midpoint m = 4 has yet to be recomputed and lies to the right of the new interval [0, 3].
frames.explanation: Since nums[4] = 6 equals the target, set j = m − 1 to check for an earlier 6. Now i = 0 and j = 3, giving the interval [0, 3]. The diagram still shows the old midpoint m = 4, just to the right of the new interval.
frames.key_state: After finding a 6, move the right boundary left: i = 0, j = 3, interval [0, 3]. The old midpoint m = 4 is outside the interval and has yet to be recomputed.
frames.title: Found a 6, so move the right boundary left

frames.announcement: Recompute the midpoint of the new interval [0, 3] as m = (0 + 3) // 2 = 1. The midpoint element nums[1] = 3 is less than the target, 6.
frames.explanation: Iteration 2: With i = 0 and j = 3, recompute the midpoint of [0, 3] as m = (0 + 3) // 2 = 1. Since nums[1] = 3 is less than the target, 6, the insertion point is to its right.
frames.key_state: Iteration 2 midpoint: i = 0, j = 3, interval [0, 3], m = 1. The value nums[1] = 3 is less than the target, 6.
frames.title: Compute midpoint 1

frames.announcement: Since nums[1] = 3 is less than the target, 6, the leftmost insertion point must be to its right. Set i = m + 1 to move the left boundary right to 2. The old midpoint m = 1 has yet to be recomputed and lies to the left of the new interval [2, 3].
frames.explanation: Since nums[1] = 3 is less than the target, 6, set i = m + 1. Now i = 2 and j = 3, giving the interval [2, 3]. The diagram still shows the old midpoint m = 1, just to the left of the new interval.
frames.key_state: After finding a 3, move the left boundary right: i = 2, j = 3, interval [2, 3]. The old midpoint m = 1 is outside the interval and has yet to be recomputed.
frames.title: Found a 3, so move the left boundary right

frames.announcement: Recompute the midpoint of [2, 3] as m = (2 + 3) // 2 = 2. The midpoint element nums[2] = 6 again equals the target, 6.
frames.explanation: Iteration 3: With i = 2 and j = 3, recompute the midpoint of [2, 3] as m = (2 + 3) // 2 = 2. Again, nums[2] = 6 equals the target.
frames.key_state: Iteration 3 midpoint: i = 2, j = 3, interval [2, 3], m = 2, nums[2] = 6.
frames.title: Compute midpoint 2

frames.announcement: Since nums[2] = 6 equals the target, 6, again set j = m − 1, giving j = 1. Now i = 2 exceeds j = 1, so the closed search interval is empty and the stopping condition holds.
frames.explanation: Since nums[2] = 6 equals the target, again set j = m − 1. Now i = 2 and j = 1. The closed interval [2, 1] is empty, so the loop will end. The diagram still shows the old midpoint m = 2, which will not be recomputed.
frames.key_state: After finding another 6, i = 2 and j = 1. The interval [2, 1] is empty. The diagram still shows the old midpoint m = 2, which will not be recomputed.
frames.title: Found another 6, leaving the interval empty

frames.announcement: The loop ends when the interval becomes empty. It returns the left boundary i = 2, where a new 6 would go before all five existing 6s. The algorithm only computes and returns the insertion index. It does not insert or move any elements in the original array.
frames.explanation: The loop ends. Only i = 2, the pointer whose index is returned, remains visible. The diagram hides j and m. Returning index 2 places the new 6 before the five existing 6s. No elements have been inserted or moved in the original array.
frames.key_state: The search ends and returns the leftmost insertion index, i = 2. The diagram hides j and m, and the original array is unchanged.
frames.title: Return the leftmost insertion index, 2

summary: When the midpoint value equals the target, keep searching to the left to find the insertion point before all equal elements.

title: Finding the leftmost insertion point with binary search
